extracted.intended_audience: writers and readers interested in composing or evaluating literary parody (parodists, poets, literary critics)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for creating and judging literary parodies (especially poetic parody): includes required authorial qualities, target-selection advice, taxonomy of parody types, and stylistic dos and don'ts. Geared toward parodists aiming for witty, tasteful imitations of established works or authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reader mindset for appreciation
rubrics_metrics.description: To enjoy parody, one must have an intense sense of the humorous and a humorous sense of the intense; this presupposes a mental attitude of wide tolerance and liberal judgments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parodies are not for those who cannot understand that parody is not necessarily ridicule. If the reader does not grasp the writer's intent, the parody has little value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary aim — amuse intelligently and cleverly
rubrics_metrics.description: The main intent of the vast majority of parodies is simply to amuse; but to amuse intelligently and cleverly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This aim is sufficiently high and should be the guiding purpose rather than attempting to justify the work by asserted moral or reforming virtues.

rubrics_metrics.name: General literary standards apply
rubrics_metrics.description: The requirements of the best parody are in a general way simply the requirements of the best literature of any sort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good parody still depends on sound literary craft; it must meet ordinary standards of good writing even as it imitates or burlesques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essential qualities of the parodist
rubrics_metrics.description: The true parodist requires an exact mental balance, a fine sense of proportion and relative values, good-humor, refinement, and unerring taste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Self-control and self-restraint are also needed; a parodist may go to the very edge, but he must not fall over. Lack of a wide, generous sense of humor combined with good taste explains why poor parodies outnumber good ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification — word-rendering (literal/word parody)
rubrics_metrics.description: Word-rendering is simply an imitation of the original, depending for its interest entirely upon the substitution of a trivial or commonplace motive for a lofty one, and following as nearly as possible the original words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such parodies burlesque the actual words of a particular poem; they are often easier to write and can be perfect of their kind (example: Lewis Carroll's 'Father William'), but are limited to parodying a specific text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification — form-rendering (style imitation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Form-rendering is the imitation of the style of an author, preferably an author given to mannerisms or affectation of some sort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This requires the parodist to imitate mannerisms and stylistic quirks rather than verbatim lines. Parodies that imitate an author's mannerisms often choose authors whose individual characteristics invite imitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification — sense-rendering (thought/mentality parody)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sense-rendering utilizes not only the original writer's diction and style, but follows a train of thought precisely along the lines that he would have pursued from the given premises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This class is by far the most meritorious: the parodist not only preserves diction and style but assimilates the author's mentality (examples: Catherine Fanshawe's imitation of Wordsworth; Calverley's 'The Cock and the Bull').

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative difficulty and merit of the three types
rubrics_metrics.description: There are three great divisions: 'word-rendering,' 'form-rendering,' and 'sense-rendering.' Sense-rendering is most meritorious; word-rendering is simplest and most literal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: More difficult than parodying a particular poem is imitating a literary style. Burlesque of mere words often fails to approximate an author's style as deeply as form- or sense-rendering can.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical skills required for style parody
rubrics_metrics.description: To accomplish imitation or burlesque of the literary style of an author, the parodist must be himself a master of style, a student of language, and possessed of a power of mimicry with an instant appreciation of opportunities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Successful form- and sense-rendering parodies require high craft: mastery of style, language sensitivity, and quick recognition of imitable traits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good targets for parody
rubrics_metrics.description: Parody is inevitable where sense is sacrificed to sound, where affectations of speech are evident, or where unwarrantable extravagance of any sort is indulged in.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such targets include authors or poems with marked mannerisms (Swinburne, Browning, Whitman, Rossetti are cited), nursery rhymes, and works whose style or excesses invite caricature. Master poets also make rich targets because their distinctive traits are prominent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mere metric/manner mimicry
rubrics_metrics.description: Parodies of the Rubaiyat often imitate Fitzgerald's version rather than Omar himself and thus are merely form-rendering—often only lines in the Rubaiyat metre—and rarely worthily done.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mere copying of metre or superficial features without capturing the author's mentality or sense often produces inferior parody.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-pattern — over-exaggeration
rubrics_metrics.description: The great fault with most parodies of Swinburne is that exaggeration is given play too freely, and the result is merely a meaningless mass of sound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exaggeration beyond restraint produces cacophony rather than clever imitation; self-restraint preserves wit and recognizability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taste, fairness, and poetic instinct
rubrics_metrics.description: The best parodies are marked by good taste, fairness, justice, and a true poetic instinct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parody should be tempered by refinement; caustic or irreverent wit (as seen in coarse ancient parodies) is often less valuable than clever, tasteful burlesque.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose and limits — parody as tribute, not reform
rubrics_metrics.description: Though defenders sometimes claim instructive or reforming value for parody, in practice it rarely causes established writers to change; parody is rather a tribute to the original's popularity and merits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not expect parody to reform authors; view it as commentary, tribute, or amusement, occasionally illuminating the original's peculiarities for readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical target-selection advice
rubrics_metrics.description: Parodies are often founded on authors whose individual characteristics invite imitation; nursery rhymes are popular themes; certain single poems (e.g., 'My Mother,' 'The Raven,' Gray's 'Elegy') show especially many parodies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selecting a well-known original increases the chance readers will recognize and appreciate the imitation; choose works with detectable mannerisms or incongruities between matter and manner.
